newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: World Bank says Bangladesh banking needs reforms.
newsitem.headline: World Bank says Bangladesh banking needs reforms.

text.p: The World Bank has urged Bangladesh to radically reform the banking sector to restore its viability and confidence in the system.

The three main "pillars" of the banking system have to be rebuilt, the World Bank Mission on (Bangladesh's) Commercial Banking Restructure said in a report. They include "an effective legal system, good management, and strong and effective central bank."

World Bank officials in Dhaka said on Friday the report was submitted to the Bangladesh government recently. It suggested that the government "should go for privatisation of national commercial banks (NCBs) only after financial restructuring is completed".
This contradicts the World Bank's earlier call for quick privatisation the NCBs.

"It is heartening that the (World Bank) mission has realised the need for establishment of strong financial infrastructure," said Toufic A. Choudhury, a member of the Bangladesh Institute of Bank Management.

Bangladesh's banking sector, especially the NCBs, has been grappling defaulted loans that led to a liquidity crisis, powerful trade unions that often disregard management on recruitment and lending, and the absence of strict laws to deal with the problems, bank officials said.
Choudhury said a law reform commission and a banking reform committee had submitted recommendations separately to beef up the banking sector. But he gave no details.
Choudhury said reforms were initiated in the banking sector as early as 1982 but "(expected) results are still far away".
The World Bank said there should be stringent legal provisions for recovery of bad debt and dealing with loan defaulters.

Current banking laws allow lengthy hearing of loan cases and provide for minimum panalties, the World Bank officials said, adding that regulations should be amended to speed trials and to allow heavier punishments.
It said the present government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, which took office in June 1996, was "having a much bigger loan default problem than that of the previous government".

Finance Ministry officials said the government inherited much of the problem from the previous regime of prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia, which they alleged "advanced fat loans to buy support of the politically biased business community".
Bangladesh NCBs recently reported being "virtually red" due to more than 130 billion taka ($3 billion) in defaulted loans, which prevented them from giving new credit for industry and other projects.
The banks were even unable to oblige when the government early this year asked them to give credit to small investors in the capital market against share certificates, bank officials said.
"Till end of May, the amount of (debt) recovery was only 20 billion taka ($460 million)," one central bank official said. ($1 = 43.5 taka)
